Empirical Research Plan: U.S. Agricultural Adaptation to Long-Run Climate Change  

====================================================================

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–way-fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (TWFE DID) with an embedded event–study.

Rationale  
•  The question is “How do *long-run* responses differ from *short-run* responses?”  Both rely on exogenous weather variation, but at different horizons.  
•  Counties east of the 100th meridian experience heterogeneous *trends* in growing-season heat and precipitation that physical science attributes largely to ocean-driven climate variability—plausibly as-good-as-random with respect to county-level agricultural decisions.  
•  TWFE lets us compare outcomes in counties that received larger positive climate shocks (treatment) with those that did not (control), before vs. after the shock.  
•  Embedding an event-study (-10 to +10 years around the “shock”) makes the parallel-trends assumption testable and yields dynamic treatment effects.  
•  Short-run elasticities come from the same specification, using *within-county* annual deviations from a 20-year moving climate mean—“weather shocks.”  
The contrast between coefficients on annual deviations (short run) and on multi-decade means (long run) reveals the degree of adaptation.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment Variable  
•  ΔHotDD_c,t: 10-year moving-average change in cumulative “extreme-heat” degree days (max temp > 29 °C) in growing season.  
•  Alternative: A multi-dimensional climate index built from principal components of HotDD and precipitation.

Treatment Definition  
•  A county-year is “treated” when its 10-year moving average crosses +1 °C-equivalent in HotDD relative to its 1950–1979 mean.  
  –  Crossing year = event time 0.  
  –  Counties that never cross the +1 °C threshold during 1980–2000 serve as never-treated controls.  

Control Group  
•  Counties whose 10-year moving average change remains within ±0.25 °C of baseline throughout 1980–2000.  
•  Event-study uses them to identify untreated counterfactual trends.  

Treatment Timing  
•  Staggered: for each county, treatment timing = first year the moving average exceeds the +1 °C threshold.  

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends (in absence of treatment): Before crossing the threshold, treated and control counties would have followed similar trends in yields, inputs, etc.  
Plausibility: Agricultural policy, technology diffusion, and market integration are largely national; region-by-year fixed effects further soak up common shocks.

A2. No Anticipation: Farmers do not change behavior *before* the climate shift is observable in the 10-year mean.  
Plausibility: Sub-decadal weather is noisy; systematic responses are unlikely before a persistent trend is recognized.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (No Spillovers): Climate experienced by one county does not affect outcomes in another (other than through equilibrium prices captured by year FE).  
Plausibility: Spatial spillovers in weather are limited by using county-level climate; price spillovers are absorbed by year FE.

A4. Exogenous Treatment Assignment: 10-year climate trends are driven by natural variability, orthogonal to county-specific shocks to productivity.  
Plausibility: Supported by attribution literature; we will still test directly (pre-trends).

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential technological adoption (e.g., heat-tolerant seed varieties) correlated with warming counties.  
   –  Mitigation: Include county-specific linear trends, interact year FE with soil type bins and with 1950–1960 mean HotDD; test robustness to excluding major seed-company test-plot counties.

T2. Policy confounding—e.g., mid-1990s crop-insurance expansion might differentially affect warmer areas.  
   –  Mitigation: Control for county-year crop-insurance take-up; allow policy-region-year FE; re-estimate on pre-1995 subsample.

T3. Selective exit of farms in hotter counties (survivorship bias).  
   –  Mitigation: (i) Census outcomes include farm counts—model extensive-margin separately.  
                 (ii) Weight yield regressions by pre-period planted area; show inverse-probability-weighted estimates that re-weight for farm exit probability.

5. R CODE OUTLINE  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # TWFE regressions
library(ggplot2)      # plots

# 1. Data -----------------------------------------------------------
dt  <- fread("county_ag_weather_1950_2005.csv")   # merged ag + climate
soil<- fread("county_soil_characteristics.csv")
dt  <- merge(dt, soil, by = "fips")

# 2. Variable Construction -----------------------------------------
# Growing-season definition: Apr 1 – Sep 30
# a. Extreme-heat degree days
dt[, HotDD := pmax(0, tmax - 29) , by = .(fips, date)]
dt[, HotDD_gs := sum(HotDD), by = .(fips, year)]

# b. 10-year moving average (long-run climate)
setorder(dt, fips, year)
dt[, HotDD10 := frollmean(HotDD_gs, 10, align = "right"), by = fips]

# c. Baseline mean (1950-1979)
base <- dt[year %between% c(1950, 1979), .(BaseHot = mean(HotDD_gs)), by = fips]
dt   <- merge(dt, base, by = "fips")
dt[, dHot10 := HotDD10 - BaseHot]           # long-run deviation
dt[, treated := as.integer(dHot10 >= 100)]  # ≈ +1 °C threshold

# d. Event time
dt[, treat_year := year[which(treated==1)[1]], by = fips]
dt[, rel_year   := year - treat_year]        # event-study leads/lags

# e. Short-run weather deviations
dt[, HotDD_dev := HotDD_gs - HotDD10]

# 3. Main Specification --------------------------------------------
# (i) Long-run adaptation (event study for corn yield)
es_formula <- log(corn_yield) ~ i(rel_year, ref = -1) |
                                fips + year

es_fit <- feols(es_formula, data = dt[rel_year %between% c(-10,10)],
                cluster = "fips")

# (ii) Short-run weather effect
sr_formula <- log(corn_yield) ~ HotDD_dev + precip_dev |
                                fips + year

sr_fit <- feols(sr_formula, data = dt, cluster = "fips")

# 4. Robustness: region-year FE + county trends
rb_formula <- log(corn_yield) ~ HotDD10 |
                                fips + region^year + fips[trend]

rb_fit <- feols(rb_formula, data = dt, cluster = "fips")

# Print summaries
etable(list("EventStudy" = es_fit,
            "ShortRun"   = sr_fit,
            "Robustness" = rb_fit))

# 5. Plot event-study coefficients
ggplot(data = broom::tidy(es_fit), 
       aes(x = as.numeric(gsub("rel_year::", "", term)), 
           y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  theme_minimal() + ylab("log Yield effect") + xlab("Years since +1 °C shock")
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Short-run: Consistent with Schlenker & Roberts (2009), a 10 °C-day increase in HotDD within a year should lower corn yield by ≈ 1–1.5 %.  

Long-run: If farmers adapt (crop choice, cultivar, irrigation, insurance), the *long-run* semi-elasticity should be **smaller in magnitude**—perhaps –0.5 % per 10 °C-day.  I expect roughly 30–50 % attenuation, i.e., one-third to one-half of the short-run effect is undone by adaptation.

Welfare implication: Projected yield losses under future warming using short-run elasticities will over-state damages; incorporating adaptation plausibly reduces predicted losses by ~40 %.

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel trends visually/empirically validated ............. 0.8  
C2: No anticipation (pre-trend flat) ............................ 0.7  
C3: No spillovers/SUTVA ........................................ 0.8  
C4: Exogeneity of treatment assignment ......................... 0.7  
C5: Stable unit composition (attrition addressed) .............. 0.6  
Average ≈ 0.72 → “moderately credible.”
